slides.direction: Second picture: what the files of the state directory mean.
slides.text:
head-name          the ref that will be moved at the end: refs/heads/feat/rerank
orig-head          where that ref pointed when the rebase started
onto               the commit that the copies are built on
git-rebase-todo    the instructions not yet executed, one per line: Git calls this the todo list
done               the instructions already executed
msgnum, end        the position: instruction 2 of 3
author-script      author name, email and date of the commit being replayed, reused for its copy
message            the commit message that will be reused when you continue
stopped-sha        the commit at which the rebase stopped
rewritten-list     "old ID, new ID" for each commit copied so far; input for the post-rewrite hook
interactive        marker of the merge backend (see the note on "git status" below)

items: Believing the branch has already moved when a rebase stops. Root cause: the branch ref is touched only when the todo list is empty; until then HEAD is detached and the branch equals ORIG_HEAD.
Deleting .git/rebase-merge to "get out". Root cause: the directory is the interpreter's state; removing it leaves HEAD detached on a half-built history, which is what --quit does deliberately.
Panicking at "interactive rebase in progress". Root cause: the default backend always writes the marker file interactive, and git status reports the file, not what you typed.
Reading ORIG_HEAD or REBASE_HEAD with cat. Root cause: since Git 2.46 they are ordinary root refs, not pseudorefs, and their storage depends on the ref format; git rev-parse reads them correctly.
Aborting after an hour of conflict resolution to "start clean". Root cause: --abort resets the working tree and the index to the old tip, and unstaged resolution edits are objects nowhere.

slides.body: A stopped rebase used to look like a broken branch.

beats.text: A colleague calls you over. Their terminal shows a wall of hints ending in "Could not apply". git branch prints the line on screen. git status says "interactive rebase in progress", and they're certain they never typed -i. They ask two things: "Have I broken the branch?" and "Is it safe to delete whatever is stuck?"
beats.tele: A colleague calls you over. Their terminal shows a wall of hints ending in "Could not apply". `git branch` prints the line on screen. `git status` says "interactive rebase in progress", and they're certain they never typed `-i`. They ask two things: "Have I broken the branch?" and "Is it safe to delete whatever is stuck?"

beats.text: The answer to the first is no, and you can prove it with one command. The answer to the second is also no, and the reason is a directory inside .git that almost nobody has opened. Today you open it. Keep both questions in mind. Each gets its proof on screen.

beats.text: In one sentence: a rebase is a small interpreter. It writes a list of instructions into a state directory inside .git, executes them one at a time on a detached HEAD, and touches the branch ref only when the list is empty.
beats.tele: In one sentence: a rebase is a small interpreter. It writes a list of instructions into a state directory inside `.git`, executes them one at a time on a detached HEAD, and touches the branch ref only when the list is empty.

beats.text: Each clause of that sentence is something you can check. On screen is today's repository before the rebase: three commits on feat/rerank, and one new commit on main.

beats.text: "A list of instructions": one line per commit, each beginning with pick. Git calls it the todo list, and the file is git-rebase-todo.
beats.tele: "A list of instructions": one line per commit, each beginning with `pick`. Git calls it the todo list, and the file is `git-rebase-todo`.

beats.text: "A state directory": .git/rebase-merge/. It exists exactly as long as a rebase is in progress. It records which ref will be moved at the end, where that ref pointed at the start, which commit the copies are built on, what has been done and what remains.
beats.tele: "A state directory": `.git/rebase-merge/`. It exists exactly as long as a rebase is in progress. It records which ref will be moved at the end, where that ref pointed at the start, which commit the copies are built on, what has been done and what remains.

beats.text: "On a detached HEAD": while the rebase runs, .git/HEAD holds a raw commit ID, not the name of a branch. HEAD walks along the new commits as they're made.
beats.tele: "On a detached HEAD": while the rebase runs, `.git/HEAD` holds a raw commit ID, not the name of a branch. HEAD walks along the new commits as they're made.

beats.text: "Touches the branch ref only when the list is empty": this is the clause people get wrong. While a rebase is stopped, the branch hasn't moved. It still names the old tip. The new commits made so far are reachable only from HEAD.

beats.text: Two consequences. First, --abort is cheap and safe: it only has to attach HEAD to the branch again, and restore the index and working tree from it. Second, if you make commits of your own during the stop, they're made on the detached HEAD. They become part of the branch only if the rebase finishes.
beats.tele: Two consequences. First, `--abort` is cheap and safe: it only has to attach HEAD to the branch again, and restore the index and working tree from it. Second, if you make commits of your own during the stop, they're made on the detached HEAD. They become part of the branch only if the rebase finishes.

beats.text: The special names. ORIG_HEAD is the tip of the branch before the rebase began. REBASE_HEAD is the commit that's being replayed right now, and it exists only while a rebase is stopped.
beats.tele: The special names. `ORIG_HEAD` is the tip of the branch before the rebase began. `REBASE_HEAD` is the commit that's being replayed right now, and it exists only while a rebase is stopped.

beats.text: The textbook attaches a version note to those names. Older behavior: the glossary called every such file, ORIG_HEAD and REBASE_HEAD included, a pseudoref, and most tutorials still do. Current behavior, since Git 2.46: "pseudoref" means only FETCH_HEAD and MERGE_HEAD, and the others are ordinary refs that live at the root of the ref namespace. Recommended: say "root ref", and read them with git rev-parse, not with cat.

Recommended: say "root ref", and read them with `git rev-parse`, not with `cat`.

beats.text: And the failure mode: deleting the state directory by hand. That leaves HEAD detached on a half-built history.
beats.tele: And the failure mode: deleting the state directory by hand. That leaves HEAD detached on a half-built history.

beats.text: A picture helps. Think of a tiny interpreter running a script. The script is the todo list. done is the part already executed, git-rebase-todo the part still to run, and msgnum and end are the program counter: instruction 2 of 3. A conflict is the interpreter pausing for input.

beats.text: The move of the branch isn't something that happens along the way. It's the last step of the script, after the last pick.
beats.tele: The move of the branch isn't something that happens along the way. It's the last step of the script, after the last `pick`.

beats.text: Where the picture breaks: a paused program usually holds its state in memory, and killing the process loses it. Git holds the state in files. You can close the terminal, restart the machine, come back the next day, and git status will read the same state directory back to you. That's also why a rebase left half done by somebody else is still sitting there, waiting.

It always writes the marker file interactive, and git status reports what it finds.

beats.text: When a rebase runs to the end, the two reflogs record it differently, as you saw in the last video. The HEAD reflog has one line per step. The branch reflog has one line for the whole rebase, and the line below it is the old tip. So <branch>@{1} means "this branch before its last rebase", and that's the most reliable undo handle you have.

beats.text: Five mistakes to watch for.
beats.tele: Five mistakes to watch for.

beats.text: Believing the branch has already moved when a rebase stops. Root cause: the branch ref is touched only when the todo list is empty; until then HEAD is detached and the branch equals ORIG_HEAD.
beats.tele: Believing the branch has already moved when a rebase stops. Root cause: the branch ref is touched only when the todo list is empty; until then HEAD is detached and the branch equals `ORIG_HEAD`.

beats.text: Deleting .git/rebase-merge to "get out". Root cause: the directory is the interpreter's state; removing it leaves HEAD detached on a half-built history, which is what --quit does deliberately.

beats.text: Panicking at "interactive rebase in progress". Root cause: the default backend always writes the marker file interactive, and git status reports the file, not what you typed.

beats.text: Reading ORIG_HEAD or REBASE_HEAD with cat. Root cause: since Git 2.46 they are ordinary root refs, not pseudorefs, and their storage depends on the ref format; git rev-parse reads them correctly.

beats.text: Aborting after an hour of conflict resolution to "start clean". Root cause: --abort resets the working tree and the index to the old tip, and unstaged resolution edits are objects nowhere.

beats.text: The textbook's routine for this is short. "Is a rebase in progress here?" The first line of git status answers it, and so does ls .git | grep rebase. If the answer is yes, nothing is lost: the branch ref hasn't moved, and git rebase --abort returns to it. Don't delete the state directory by hand.
